before_FAQ: The name is a shortened form of \"Arts Décoratifs,\" part of the formal French title given to the 1925 event that historians now point to as the style's launch point. But that event never used the abbreviation. \"Art Déco\" wasn't used publicly to label the movement until a 1966 museum retrospective in Paris, and it settled in as the go-to English term only once Bevis Hillier's defining 1968 book on the style came out.

Contemporaries at the time referred to the style by its French name, roughly \"the modern style\"; for its more machine-influenced strand they said \"Jazz Moderne\" instead. In English-language writing it was more often called \"Art Moderne\" instead. None of these earlier labels stuck as the name people use for the style today.

Britannica dates the style's international run from 1919 to 1939, with its best-known monuments concentrated in the 1920s and early 1930s. The style is most associated with that window even though, as with the label itself, exact start and end dates vary by source and by medium.

A department-appointed commission attended anyway and reported back in 1926 that the decision had misread what the event actually required.

Yes. Designed by William Van Alen, it was finished on 27 May 1930. It remains widely cited as one of the style's defining monuments, built by the same country that had skipped official participation in that same Paris exposition just five years earlier. The Empire State, taller by roughly 200 feet, finished construction on 11 April 1931 and formally opened on 1 May 1931.

Britannica traces the style's design DNA to Cubism, the Bauhaus, the Ballets Russes, and Art Nouveau, along with early Classical, Egyptian, and American Indian influences plus stylised natural motifs. The 1922 unearthing of Tutankhamun's burial chamber specifically fed the Egyptian-derived elements, scarabs, lotus columns and sunburst fans, that surfaced in jewellery and architecture during the years right after the find.

No, and they don't overlap much in time either. Art Nouveau ran from roughly 1880 to 1914 and drew on nature, favoring sinuous curves, floral motifs, and asymmetrical organic forms. Art Deco followed after World War I and looked to the machine age instead, favoring sharp angles, geometric symmetry, and streamlined forms, with its own coming-out moment at that 1925 Paris event that later gave the style its name.

In architecture, historians usually group Art Deco buildings into three styles: Zigzag Moderne, the earlier, heavily decorated 1920s style built around geometric ornamentation; Classic Moderne, a more restrained, symmetrical variant; and Streamline Moderne, the 1930s style borrowed from aerodynamic design, built around smooth curves and horizontal speed lines.

New York's Chrysler skyscraper, designed by William Van Alen and completed in 1930, is the piece most often pointed to, with a stainless-steel, sunburst-patterned spire and eagle gargoyles at the setbacks. The Empire State and Radio City Music Hall, both also in New York, are usually the next two cited.

before_FAQ: Each surviving daguerreotype stands alone: nothing else quite like it exists, since its image formed straight onto a silver-coated copper plate, not printed from any negative. Producing one took several chemical stages: iodine sensitizing, camera exposure, and mercury-vapor development, then a fixing bath. The resulting silver surface scratched and tarnished so easily that a finished plate usually ended up behind glass in a protective case.

Louis Daguerre spent the 1830s in Paris refining the process, picking up where his earlier collaboration with Nicéphore Niépce had left off, and made his process public in a formal announcement dated August 19, 1839. Descriptions of this exact plate had already reached American newspapers within weeks of that announcement.

Exposure times fell dramatically as the process matured: Niépce's earlier heliograph technique from the 1820s needed roughly eight hours, while Daguerre's refined technique by 1838 typically ran about four or five minutes. For this plate specifically, though, sources disagree: some place it in that same four-to-five-minute window, others put the same shot at ten to fifteen minutes, and nobody has settled which figure is correct.

That's the popular claim, but it stands on shakier ground than the caption suggests. Even the date is unresolved (1837 or 1838), researchers have questioned whether the figures typically identified as a bootblack and his customer could actually be something stationary, like a water pump, and a 2010 close analysis turned up more faint traces in the frame than the standard two-figure story accounts for. There's also a rival claim to the title: Hippolyte Bayard claimed self-portraits dating back to 1837, a year earlier, but every one of those plates is gone, leaving no way to confirm it.

After surviving the March 1839 fire at Daguerre's studio, the plate was given as a gift to Bavaria's king that same October, then sat largely forgotten in storage for close to a hundred years. Beaumont Newhall tracked it down again in the mid-1930s and produced copy prints for a New York show; a later attempt to fix up the plates in Munich, in 1970, went badly and left them further damaged. Virtually every image of this photograph you'll encounter today, this article's opening picture included, comes from Newhall's decades-old copies; the plate itself was never rescanned afterward.

Cost and convenience beat it out. By the late 1850s, portrait studios were switching over to the ambrotype, a glass-based process that was quicker and cheaper to produce. Daguerreotypes also had a deeper structural problem: since each plate was an unrepeatable, one-shot original with no negative behind it, getting a second copy meant sitting for a second exposure, unlike rival processes built around a negative, which could print as many copies as anyone wanted from a single sitting.

Tilt it. A daguerreotype's image sits on a mirror-polished sheet of silvered copper, so from one angle it reads as a dark negative and from another, held at roughly 45 degrees, the correct positive image appears, an effect neither paper photographs nor the ambrotypes and tintypes that came after it in the market can reproduce. Most surviving examples are also small and kept sealed in a hinged case behind glass with a brass mat, since the exposed metal darkens and scuffs quickly in open air.

Most are worth relatively little: ordinary studio portraits with no case or identified sitter trade at flea-market levels. Value climbs sharply for pieces with a named subject, an intact case and seal, an unusual size, or a rare subject beyond the standard studio portrait; outdoor and occupational scenes are especially sought after.

Daguerreotype is one specific, early photographic process, not a synonym for photograph in general. It produces a direct positive image on a silver-coated copper plate, skipping the negative stage entirely, so the plate itself is the only copy that will ever exist unless the sitter poses again; most later photographic processes, film and digital alike, are built around a negative or file that can be reprinted any number of times. Its mirror-polished plate also behaves differently from a printed photograph: tilted at the right angle, the image flips between a dark negative and a correct positive, an effect paper prints can't reproduce.

It reached the public before any rival process existed. Louis Daguerre unveiled it in a formal announcement dated 19 August 1839, building on years of earlier work alongside Nicéphore Niépce. Historians generally mark it as the moment photography went public: within weeks, newspapers as far away as the United States were describing the process, and portrait studios using it opened in cities across Europe and North America within a year or two. It stayed the leading way to buy a photograph for roughly twenty years, until cheaper glass-based methods like the ambrotype took over in the late 1850s.

before_FAQ: At least six well-known names started as put-downs from critics or rival schools: Impressionism (Louis Leroy's coinage, 1874), Fauvism (Louis Vauxcelles, 1905), Cubism (Vauxcelles again, 1908), Rococo (coined pejoratively in the 1790s), Baroque (used as a term of abuse through much of the eighteenth century), and Gothic (Vasari's 1550 book of artist biographies dismissed it in near-identical terms).

Paris critic Louis Leroy, writing up the group's first exhibition for Le Charivari, ran his mocking piece the same week the show opened in spring 1874, aimed at Claude Monet's Le Havre harbor canvas. By their third group show in 1877, the painters were using that same word themselves as its official title.

Vauxcelles, who had already coined the Fauves' name, wrote that Braque's 1908 landscapes painted at L'Estaque, rejected by the Salon d'Automne jury and shown instead at dealer Kahnweiler's own gallery, reduced everything to \"cubes,\" in his Gil Blas write-up that same November. Vauxcelles said the exact image came from Henri Matisse, who'd used it in conversation about the rejected paintings.

Giorgio Vasari pinned the blame for pointed arches and ribbed vaults on the Goths as an insult in his 1550 Lives of the Artists, but the timeline does not hold up. Byzantine forces ended Ostrogothic rule in Italy in 553, and Muslim conquest ended Visigothic rule in Spain in 711, both events centuries before historians date the style's actual debut to Abbot Suger's rebuilt choir outside Paris, consecrated in 1144.

It started as one. Portuguese and Spanish jewelers used the word for an irregular, misshapen pearl, and critics a century on borrowed that same put-down for seventeenth-century painting and buildings, favoring Neoclassical restraint instead. Credit for turning it into a neutral style category generally goes to Heinrich Wölfflin, a Swiss scholar whose 1888 study of the two periods' contrasting formal logic is how art historians still use the word today.

before_FAQ: A building or built structure, rather than a person, narrative event, or open landscape, has to be the primary subject the composition is organized around for a piece to count as this genre rather than a painting that simply includes a building somewhere in it. It developed through invented perspective exercises in the 16th century, then Dutch church interiors and Italian view painting in the 17th and 18th centuries, and later Romantic ruin views and 19th-century watercolor topography, per its own historical account on Wikipedia.

Credit for founding the genre usually goes to Vredeman de Vries. Active mainly in the Low Countries in the second half of the 16th century, this Dutch-born artist and theorist built it through his printed perspective series, beginning with the 1560 Scenographiae set, work that Dumbarton Oaks' collection notes describe as invented city and building views, not depictions of real places.

Yes, in the sense that mattered to his reputation: the Rijksmuseum contrasts him with predecessors who favored invented, imaginary churches, noting that Saenredam always worked from existing buildings and described his process as working 'after life.' But London's museum record for his Grote Kerk, Haarlem painting shows that he still made significant proportional changes to those real buildings once he moved from his measured drawings to the final panel.

A veduta is a view painting based on an identifiable real place, even when, as with Canaletto's paintings of Venice's main square, the perspective or exact measurements have been adjusted. Also called a capriccio, this second category makes no claim to depict one real location at all; curators note that Guardi's Venetian caprice combines a clock-tower archway with courtyard buildings borrowed from the Doge's Palace, features from separate real buildings assembled into a place that never existed as painted.

London's museum record for his Piazza San Marco painting says Canaletto habitually gave the bell tower more height and a slimmer profile than the real structure carried, describing the change as part of a broader set of intentional design decisions, including an exaggerated perspective angle across the square, not a measurement error. A taller, more slender tower reads as a stronger vertical anchor against the square's horizontal sweep of arcades.

before_FAQ: Also called the Piedra del Sol, this Aztec Sun Stone monument is a massive stone disc weighing over 24 metric tons, made by Mexica artisans sometime around 1502 to 1520. It spans roughly 3.6 meters across, sits today in the Mexican capital's national anthropology museum, and turned up during Zócalo repaving work on 17 December 1790.

Not in a functional, day-to-day sense. Its outer rings do display markers for each of the 20 days in the Aztec solar cycle, which is why 18th- and 19th-century writers gave it the popular nickname \u2018Calendar Stone,\u2019 but those markers track cyclical time symbolically rather than real dates. Current thinking at its home museum favors a sacrificial function tied to gladiatorial combat, not a timekeeping one.

Scholars disagree. Researchers working in the early 1900s first linked the face to Tonatiuh, the sun god, and that reading stuck as the monument's popular name. In 1974, two other scholars pointed instead to Tlaltecuhtli, an earth deity, a view that Richard Townsend also held, laid out in his 1979 book on Aztec imperial art. A third possibility, put forward by Cecilia Klein in 1976, names a deity called Yohualtecuhtli (the 'night sun') and David Stuart, who studies Maya writing, added a fourth idea in 2016: that the same face might double as a symbolic portrait of Moctezuma II, the reigning Mexica ruler, worked into the surrounding glyph.

There's no direct evidence that it did. In modern scholarship, the Vienna object goes by the Nahuatl name quetzalāpanecayōtl outlined in a paper by Zelia Nuttall that reads its shape as a feathered bird form. The piece's link to Moctezuma II, though, rests on tradition, not documentation. One Harvard-based art historian has pointed out that Mexica royalty apparently kept a wardrobe of different crowns, rarely repeating one, which makes it hard to pin one surviving piece definitively on a specific ruler.

Conservators from Mexico and Austria spent 2010 to 2012 jointly examining and preserving the feathered headdress, and found it too fragile for the shaking and temperature swings of transport, so it stays put, even though Mexico's most recent formal appeal for its return came in 2020. The object is still in Vienna, and a 1940 replica stands in for it at the Mexico City institution that holds the original Sun Stone.
